title: The Namdharis today
hook: they keep white dress and simple rites, and differ from most Sikhs in following a living guru

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nanaksar tradition, where readers and singers hand the Guru's word on in turns. Your line was continuous praise. What did you keep going with someone else? Day one thousand three hundred fourteen.

A wedding in a courtyard, and everyone is in white. The men's turbans are white too, tied flat and straight across the forehead. There is no great feast of display, no long line of expensive gifts. A small sacred fire is lit, hymns are sung, and a couple is married simply. Some guests hold a mala, a string of beads, made of white wool. If you know Sikh weddings from photos of crimson and gold, this one may look like a different world. It belongs to the Namdharis, and today we meet them on their own terms.
screen: `A WEDDING ALL IN WHITE.` → `A SMALL FIRE, HYMNS, A SIMPLE RITE.` → `A WOOL MALA IN THE HAND.`

segments.voice: The Namdharis are a Sikh community whose name carries naam, the Name of God, at its center: those who hold to the Name. Year three told how the movement took shape, with Satguru Ram Singh, his call to simple living, and his stand against British rule that ended in exile. They're also called Kukas, and tradition links that name to the cries of devotion that rose in their gatherings. Today they keep three marks. White clothing, plain and often handspun, with the turban tied in their own straight style. Simple rites: weddings without dowry or display, around a small fire with hymns. And a strict life of vegetarian food and daily remembrance of the Name, with the wool mala close at hand. Then the difference, stated plainly. The wider panth holds that the line of human Gurus ended with Guru Gobind Singh, and that the Guru is now the Granth and the Khalsa together. Namdharis follow a living guru, a line of satgurus who lead the community today. That's a real difference, and Sikhs on both sides of it take it seriously. This path won't argue it out. What it can do is listen to the Granth that both sides revere. Guru Arjan, in Raag Kanra on Ang 1299, sings, in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone. That line doesn't erase disagreement. It sets a tone for living beside it. A difference can be named clearly, held honestly, and still met with respect.
screen: `NAMDHARI: THOSE WHO HOLD TO THE NAME.` · `WHITE DRESS AND SIMPLE RITES.` · `THE DIFFERENCE: A LIVING GURU.` · `ANG 1299: NO ENEMY, NO STRANGER.` · then, large: `DIFFERENT, AND RESPECTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect a difference. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person whose faith or way of life differs from yours on something that matters. Don't rehearse the argument. Say the difference to yourself once, plainly, in a single sentence, the way they'd want it said. Then breathe in, and notice one thing in them you can honestly respect. Breathe out, and let both stand side by side. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
The Namdharis today. A Sikh community known for white dress, simple rites and a strict life of the Name, which follows a living guru. Today's word.

Your line: different, and respected. Today, when you notice someone doing a thing differently, say the difference in your head the way they'd say it, before you say anything out loud. Day one thousand three hundred fourteen.
